terms.grammar: verb, second conjugation, semi-deponent: with an accusative and infinitive, with quod, or with the ablative of the thing
evidence: Cic. Fam. 6.19.1: Maculam officiō fūnctum esse gaudeō.
terms.comment: “I’m glad” is a verb in Latin, not an adjective: gaudeō tē vēnisse, I’m glad you came. It is the everyday word of Terence and of Cicero’s letters, often with vehementer, “very”.

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, deponent: with quod, an accusative and infinitive, or the ablative
evidence: Cic. Fam. 2.1.2: et laetor, quod absēns omnia cum maximā dignitāte es cōnsecūtus
terms.comment: Beside gaudeō in Cicero’s letters, of a joy that shows; it can also mean “rejoice” in a solemn sense (Lewis & Short).
The adjective, mostly of how someone looks or is (see happy); for “I’m glad that …” Latin uses the verb. Of crops and fields it means rich, flourishing (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: phrase: the adverb volup with est, the person in the dative
terms.comment: Old and comic, the opposite of aegrē est, “I’m sorry, it upsets me”.

phrases.english: I don’t regret it. — I’m glad.
I’m glad Macula has done his duty.

phrases.latin: tē istīc invītum nōn esse vehementer gaudeō
phrases.english: I’m very glad you don’t mind being there

phrases.latin: nam quia vōs tranquillōs videō, gaudeō et volup est mihi.
phrases.english: for since I see you calm, I’m glad and pleased.
